result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Validate.to_json_schema()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Export this validation plan as a JSON Schema document. twitter-card: title: >- [Validate.to_json_schema()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Export this validation plan as a JSON Schema document. title: >- [Validate.to_json_schema()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Export this validation plan as a JSON Schema document. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Export this validation plan as a JSON Schema document. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/validate.py#L20037-L20144){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Validate.to_json_schema(path=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The `to_json_schema()` method walks the validation steps and maps each one to its closest JSON Schema equivalent. This lets you share your validation rules as a portable, language-neutral schema that tools across many ecosystems can consume. When the `Validate` object has data attached, the schema is enriched with column type information inferred from the data (e.g., `"type": "integer"` for Int64 columns). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [path]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | Path | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : An optional file path. If provided, the JSON Schema is written to this file (parent directories are created as needed) in addition to being returned. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[str, Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The JSON Schema document as a dictionary. This is a valid JSON Schema that can be serialized with `json.dumps()` or consumed by any JSON Schema validator. ::: ## Supported Mappings {.doc-supported-mappings} The following validation methods have direct JSON Schema equivalents: | Pointblank method | JSON Schema keyword | |---|---| | `col_vals_not_null()` | `required` | | `col_vals_gt()` | `exclusiveMinimum` | | `col_vals_ge()` | `minimum` | | `col_vals_lt()` | `exclusiveMaximum` | | `col_vals_le()` | `maximum` | | `col_vals_eq()` | `const` | | `col_vals_in_set()` | `enum` | | `col_vals_between()` | `minimum` + `maximum` | | `col_vals_regex()` | `pattern` | | `col_vals_within_spec()` | `format` | Steps with no JSON Schema equivalent (e.g., `rows_distinct()`, `tbl_match()`, `col_vals_outside()`) are silently skipped. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Let's write a validation plan for a table of user accounts and export it as JSON Schema. ::: {#13493087 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import polars as pl import json accounts = pl.DataFrame( { "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Chloé"], "age": [34, 27, 45], "status": ["active", "inactive", "active"], } ) validation = ( pb.Validate(data=accounts) .col_vals_gt(columns="age", value=0) .col_vals_not_null(columns="name") .col_vals_in_set(columns="status", set=["active", "inactive"]) .rows_distinct() ) schema = validation.to_json_schema() print(json.dumps(schema, indent=2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema", "type": "object", "properties": { "age": { "exclusiveMinimum": 0, "type": "integer" }, "name": { "type": "string" }, "status": { "enum": [ "active", "inactive" ], "type": "string" } }, "required": [ "name" ] } ``` ::: ::: Each column has a property: `age > 0` became `exclusiveMinimum`, the set of statuses became `enum`, and the not-null check on `name` put it in `required`. The `type` of each property comes from the data attached to the plan. The [`rows_distinct()`](`pointblank.Validate.rows_distinct`) step has no JSON Schema equivalent (a schema describes one record at a time), so it isn't in the output. Since the result is a standard schema, it can be given to any JSON Schema validator, for example to check records in an API before they're loaded into the table. With `path=`, the schema is also written to a file.
